title: XL Airways Germany 888T

agencies.name: Bureau of Enquiry and Analysis for Civil Aviation Safety
agencies.report_title: Accident on 27 November 2008 off the coast of Canet-Plage to the Airbus A320-232 registered D-AXLA

summary: XL Airways Flight 888T, an Airbus A320 acceptance flight, crashed into the Mediterranean Sea on 27 November 2008 near Canet-en-Roussillon. Maintenance personnel had failed to protect angle-of-attack (AOA) sensors during aircraft rinsing three days prior, allowing water to penetrate and freeze inside the sensors. During a low-speed check near 2,900 feet, the blocked sensors rendered angle-of-attack protections inoperative. The crew descended below planned altitude and stalled the aircraft, entered direct flight control law, and were unable to recover despite multiple control inputs and maximum thrust.
probable_cause: The accident was caused by the loss of control of the aeroplane by the crew following the improvised demonstration of the functioning of the angle of attack protections, while the blockage of the angle of attack sensors made it impossible for these protections to trigger. The crew was not aware of the blockage of the angle of attack sensors. They did not take into account the speeds mentioned in the programme of checks available to them and consequently did not stop the demonstration before the stall (p. 98). Contributing factors included the decision to carry out the demonstration at low height, the crew's inadequate management of the strong pitch increase, the increased workload from managing adapted in-flight checks, and the absence of protection for AOA sensors during rinsing operations (p. 99).

factors.evidence: Maintenance personnel performed aircraft rinsing with fresh water on 24 November 2008 without following proper rinsing procedures and without protecting angle-of-attack sensors (p. 96)

Water penetrated inside angle-of-attack sensors 1 and 2 during rinsing and remained there until freezing during the accident flight three days later (p. 96). AOA sensors 1 and 2 blocked between 15:04 and 15:06 at identical local angle-of-attack values consistent with cruise angle of attack, rendering protections inoperative in normal law (p. 97)

The crew decided to undertake the low-speed protection check at approximately 4,000 ft altitude without preparation and without reading theoretical minimum speeds from the flight check program (p. 97). The check should have been performed at FL140 per the Airbus Customer Acceptance Manual (p. 96)

The airplane crashed completely into the Mediterranean Sea with all seven occupants killed. Due to the stabilizer position at full pitch-up and the pitch-up moment generated by engines at maximum thrust, crew lost control during thrust increase and could not recover (p. 98)
Aircraft stalled at approximately 99 kt speed in landing configuration when attempting to test angle-of-attack protections at low altitude (p. 18)

events.text: On 24 November 2008, aircraft rinsed with fresh water to eliminate dust from fuselage without following rinsing task procedure and without protecting angle-of-attack sensors (p. 96)
Aircraft D-AXLA ferried to Perpignan aerodrome on 3 November 2008 for maintenance and painting work (p. 16)
Aircraft left ramp at Perpignan aerodrome. Flight plan filed as GXL888T with planned flight time of 2 hours 35 minutes over west of France (p. 16)
Air New Zealand pilot introduced himself and asked crew to raise hand if he interrupted during flight checks (p. 16)

Takeoff from runway 21 at Perpignan with Captain as pilot flying and co-pilot as pilot non-flying. On board: 2 XL Airways pilots, 1 Air New Zealand pilot in cockpit, 3 Air New Zealand engineers, 1 NZ CAA representative (p. 16)
CRNA south-west controller contacted Perpignan approach controller by phone, expressing concern about flight described as 'disguised test flight' without proper authorization (p. 16)
Captain requested to perform a '360' turn; controller explained this maneuver could not be undertaken in general air traffic as filed flight plan did not include it (p. 16)
Captain proposed to Air New Zealand pilot to delay check on flight controls to approach phase (p. 16)
Crew cleared to climb to FL320, which they reached two minutes later (p. 17)

Between 15:04 and 15:06, angle-of-attack sensors 1 and 2 stopped moving and remained blocked at almost identical local angles of attack of 4.2 and 3.8 degrees respectively, consistent with cruise angle of attack (p. 17)
Crew began descent to FL310 (p. 17)
Captain performed flight control checks in normal law (p. 17)
While waiting for clearance to climb to FL390, Air New Zealand pilot noted few checks remaining and said APU check could be done during return flight to Frankfurt (p. 17)
Aircraft reached FL390 (p. 17)
Descent towards Perpignan initiated (p. 17)
Crew cleared to descend to FL130. Eighteen seconds later, Air New Zealand pilot asked if crew ready to perform flight control check in alternate law (p. 17)
Crew contacted Perpignan Approach, were cleared to descend to FL120 towards PPG VOR, instructed to reduce speed to 250 kt (p. 17)
At FL120, captain asked 'you want alternate law' and New Zealand pilot answered 'okay alternate law' (p. 17)

Flight control laws in pitch and roll returned to normal law, indicating end of alternate law check. Autopilot 1 reconnected. Air New Zealand pilot then mentioned low-speed flight would be next (p. 17)
Approach controller asked crew to descend to FL60. Aircraft slightly below FL100, speed 214 kt. Five seconds later, co-pilot asked to engage wing anti-ice at approximately 9,900 ft (p. 17-18)
Approach controller asked crew to turn right to heading 190 and maintain 180 kt. About one minute later cleared to LANET-ILS approach for runway 33 and descend to 5,000 ft (p. 18)
Aircraft reached 5,000 ft altitude at approximately 210 kt (p. 18)
Approach controller asked aircraft speed. Co-pilot initially answered speed falling, then at 15:42:25 said 180 kt. Actual speed slightly above 190 kt (p. 18)
Spoilers deployed between 15:43:20 and 15:43:55 (p. 18)
'Triple click' recorded, AP/FD lateral mode changed from NAV to HDG at heading 090. Aircraft at 2,940 ft altitude, speed 107 kt (Vmin) (p. 18)
Captain disengaged autopilot saying 'Down below the clouds so you want what?' Thirty seconds later positioned thrust control levers on IDLE and autothrust disengaged at 4,080 ft, speed 166 kt (p. 18)
Captain stabilized aircraft at 3,000 ft in landing configuration. Flight directors active, vertical mode OP DES to V/S +0000. Speed was 136 kt (p. 18)
Aircraft at 2,980 ft altitude, speed 123.5 kt (VLS). Stabilizer moved from -4.4° to -11.2° corresponding to electric pitch-up stop (p. 18)
Aircraft at 2,910 ft altitude, speed 99 kt. Pitch angle 18.6 degrees. Stall warning sounded for first time. Limit speeds Vαprot and Vαmax underestimated due to blocked AOA sensors (p. 18, 97)
Thrust control levers moved to TO/GA position. Symmetrical increase in engine RPM to approximately 88% N1. Aircraft began to roll left (p. 18)
Bank angle reached 8° left, speed 92.5 kt. Captain countered with lateral input to right and longitudinal input forward (p. 19)
Wings straightened and began roll right. Captain made lateral input to left stop, rudder began moving for left turn (p. 19)
Both flight directors disengaged. At 15:45:14, autothrust disarmed (p. 19)
Flight control laws switched from normal law to direct law. Bank reached 50° right. Pitch 11°, speed 100 kt, altitude approximately 2,580 ft. Elevators at maximum nose-down position 11.6° (p. 19)
Stall warning stopped. Bank angle 40° left. Aircraft pitch 7°, wings nearly horizontal, speed 138 kt (p. 19)
Pitch and altitude began to increase to approximately 2,250 ft. Speed dropped, stall warning sounded again at 15:45:36 (p. 19-20)
Landing gear retracted. Pitch reached maximum 52° nose-up, bank angle maximum 59° left, normal load factor below 0.5g (p. 20)
Speed dropped below 40 kt (p. 20)
Maximum values recorded: pitch 57° nose-up, altitude 3,788 ft (p. 20)
Stall warning stopped, started again approximately 5 seconds later (p. 20)
Captain made longitudinal pitch-up input. Between 15:45:49 and 15:45:53, elevator reached values of 30° pitch-up (p. 20)
Normal load factor exceeded 0.5g. Thrust control levers placed in CLIMB position for one second then repositioned to TO/GA (p. 20)
From 15:45:52, speed passed above 40 kt. At 15:45:53, pitch 7° nose-down, bank less than 10° left (p. 20)
Between 15:45:55 and 15:45:58, captain made lateral input to left stop; aircraft rolled right. Bank angle from 3° to 97°, pitch from 3° nose-down to 42° nose-down (p. 20)
From 15:45:57, captain's longitudinal input nose-up; elevator at 14.5° nose-down (p. 20)
Flaps and slats selected to position 1, then position 0 two seconds later (p. 20)
Stall warning stopped, followed by CRC warning (Master Warning) which stopped two seconds later. Pitch reached maximum 51° nose-down, bank 45° right, speed 183 kt, altitude 1,620 ft (p. 20)
Thrust levers moved back to near IDLE, then advanced to CLIMB position. EPR on two engines dropped to 1.2 then increased to 1.25 (p. 20)
EGPWS TERRAIN TERRAIN warning recorded, followed one second later by another CRC warning (Master Warning) (p. 20)

Flight data recordings stopped. Last recorded values: pitch 14° nose-down, bank 15° right, speed 263 kt, altitude 340 ft. Between first stall warning and end of recording, 62 seconds had elapsed. Aircraft crashed into Mediterranean Sea at approximately 7 km off French coast near Canet-en-Roussillon (p. 20)

recommendations.text: Detail in EU-OPS the various types of non-revenue flights that operators are authorized to perform
Require non-revenue flights be described precisely in approved operations manuals, specifying preparation, program, operational framework, crew qualifications and training
As temporary measure, require non-revenue flights be subject to authorization or operator declaration on case-by-case basis
Ensure that equipment installation conditions during certification tests performed by equipment manufacturers are representative of those on the aircraft
Undertake a safety study to improve certification standards of warning systems for crews during flight control system reconfigurations or training in identifying these reconfigurations
In cooperation with manufacturers, improve training exercises and techniques relating to approach-to-stall to ensure control of the aircraft in the pitch axis
